claim: Physically identical nociceptive input can lead to variable sensations of pain, depending on contextual factors.
source: It has been shown that physically identical nociceptive input can lead to variable sensations of pain, depending on contextual factors (Tracey and Mantyh, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tracey and Mantyh, 2007

claim: Attention, reappraisal, and expectation are core mechanisms that influence how nociception leads to pain.
source: In particular, attention, reappraisal, and expectation are core mechanisms that influence how nociception leads to pain (Wiech et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wiech et al., 2008

claim: Placebo hypoalgesia is pain relief mediated by expectation and experience in the absence of active treatment.
source: A clinically important example of how expectations can shape pain processing is placebo hypoalgesia: pain relief mediated by expectation and experience – in the absence of active treatment (Petrovic et al., 2002; Wager et al., 2004; Colloca and Benedetti, 2005; Bingel et al., 2006; Atlas and Wager, 2012; Anchisi and Zanon, 2015).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to studies on placebo hypoalgesia

claim: Pain perception can be seen as the consequence of an integration of expectations with nociception in the context of a generative model.
source: In the context of a generative model of pain, it has been proposed that pain perception can be seen as the consequence of an integration of expectations with nociception (Büchel et al., 2014; Wiech, 2016; Ongaro and Kaptchuk, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to theoretical frameworks

claim: Expectations are integrated with incoming nociceptive information and both are weighted by their relative precision to form a pain percept.
source: In this framework, expectations are integrated with incoming nociceptive information and both are weighted by their relative precision (Grahl et al., 2018) to form a pain percept.
evidence: Supported by citation to Grahl et al., 2018

claim: Phasic gamma activity has been associated with stimulus intensity over the sensory cortex.
source: Generally, phasic gamma activity has been associated with stimulus intensity over the sensory cortex where the amplitudes of pain-induced gamma oscillations increase with objective stimulus intensity and subjective pain intensity (Gross et al., 2007; Hauck et al., 2007; Zhang et al., 2012; Rossiter et al., 2013; Tiemann et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to EEG studies

claim: Pain-related gamma band oscillations have been linked to the insular cortex as well as temporal and frontal regions.
source: Additionally, pain-related gamma band oscillations have been linked to the insular cortex as well as temporal and frontal regions using depth electrodes in epilepsy patients (Liberati et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Liberati et al., 2018

claim: Gamma activity is enhanced by attention in visual, auditory, sensorimotor processing, and nociception.
source: In addition, gamma activity is enhanced by attention in human EEG experiments in visual (Gruber et al., 1999), auditory (Tiitinen et al., 1993; Debener et al., 2003), and sensorimotor processing (i.e. tactile stimuli) (Bauer et al., 2006) as well as in nociception (Hauck et al., 2007; Hauck et al., 2015; Tiemann et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations across different sensory modalities

claim: Pain-related alpha-to-beta band oscillations are typically suppressed with higher stimulus intensity.
source: Pain-related alpha-to-beta band oscillations are typically found to be suppressed with higher stimulus intensity (Mouraux et al., 2003; Ploner et al., 2006; May et al., 2012; Hu et al., 2013), which is enhanced by attention (May et al., 2012) and (placebo) expectation (Huneke et al., 2013; Tiemann et al., 2015; Albu and Meagher, 2016).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to EEG studies

claim: Prestimulus theta, alpha, and gamma activity can affect subsequent pain processing.
source: Interestingly, prestimulus theta (Taesler and Rose, 2016) as well as prestimulus alpha and gamma activity (Tu et al., 2016) can affect subsequent pain processing.
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on prestimulus activity

claim: Trials with smaller prestimulus alpha and gamma oscillations were perceived as more painful.
source: Specifically, trials with smaller prestimulus alpha and gamma oscillations were perceived as more painful, suggesting a negative modulation of subsequent pain perception (Tu et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tu et al., 2016

claim: The anterior insular cortex plays an important role in mediating expectation effects and the integration of prior expectation and prediction errors in pain.
source: Previous functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) studies have suggested an important role of the anterior insular cortex for mediating expectation effects and the integration of prior expectation and prediction errors in the context of pain (Ploghaus et al., 1999; Koyama et al., 2005; Atlas et al., 2010; Geuter et al., 2017; Fazeli and Büchel, 2018).
evidence: Supported by multiple fMRI study citations

claim: Neuronal signals in the anterior insula represent predictions and prediction errors with respect to pain.
source: These studies have revealed that neuronal signals in the anterior insula represent predictions and prediction errors with respect to pain, which in theory would allow the combination of both terms as required for predictive coding (Büchel et al., 2014; Ongaro and Kaptchuk, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to fMRI studies and theoretical frameworks

claim: In fMRI studies, predictions and prediction errors cannot be temporally dissociated due to the low temporal resolution of the method.
source: However, in fMRI studies, predictions and prediction errors cannot be temporally dissociated due to the low temporal resolution of the method.
evidence: Based on known limitations of fMRI methodology

claim: The study employed contact heat stimuli with three different intensities (low heat, medium heat, and high heat), preceded by a visual cue indicating the upcoming intensity.
source: In this experiment (N = 29) we employed contact heat stimuli with three different intensities (low heat, medium heat, and high heat), preceded by a visual cue indicating the upcoming intensity (Figure 1).
evidence: Describes the experimental design used in the study

claim: The modality was correctly cued in 70% of all trials and stimulus intensities were correctly cued in 60% of all trials.
source: To generate prediction errors, the modality (picture or heat) was correctly cued only in 70% of all trials, and stimulus intensities were correctly cued only in 60% of all trials.
evidence: Describes the experimental manipulation to generate prediction errors

claim: Alpha-to-beta activity was associated with stimulus intensity expectation.
source: Our data show that alpha-to-beta activity was associated with stimulus intensity expectation, followed by a negative modulation of gamma band activity by absolute prediction errors.
evidence: Main finding from the EEG data analysis

claim: Gamma band activity was negatively modulated by absolute prediction errors.
source: Our data show that alpha-to-beta activity was associated with stimulus intensity expectation, followed by a negative modulation of gamma band activity by absolute prediction errors.
evidence: Main finding from the EEG data analysis

claim: Prediction errors in visual and auditory perception are associated with increased gamma band activity.
source: This is in contrast to prediction errors in visual and auditory perception, which are associated with increased gamma band activity, but is in agreement with observations in working memory and word matching, which show gamma band activity for correct, rather than violated, predictions.
evidence: Comparison with findings from other sensory modalities

claim: Observations in working memory and word matching show gamma band activity for correct, rather than violated, predictions.
source: This is in contrast to prediction errors in visual and auditory perception, which are associated with increased gamma band activity, but is in agreement with observations in working memory and word matching, which show gamma band activity for correct, rather than violated, predictions.
evidence: Comparison with findings from other cognitive domains

claim: Expectation signals should temporally precede prediction error signals.
source: Based on the previous data, we hypothesized that expectation signals should temporally precede prediction error signals.
evidence: Hypothesis based on theoretical considerations

claim: Prediction error signals should be related to higher frequencies (e.g. gamma band) than prediction signals.
source: Based on the functional neuroanatomy of cortical microcircuits (Bastos et al., 2012), with feedforward connections predominately originating from superficial layers and feedback connections from deep layers, we expect that prediction error signals should be related to higher frequencies (e.g. gamma band) than prediction signals (Todorovic et al., 2011; Arnal and Giraud, 2012).
evidence: Hypothesis based on microcircuit theory and citations

claim: The study investigated 35 healthy male participants (mean 26, range 18–37 years).
source: We investigated 35 healthy male participants (mean 26, range 18–37 years), who were paid as compensation for their participation.
evidence: Description of study participants

claim: Data from six participants had to be excluded from the final EEG data analysis due to technical issues, leaving a final sample of 29 participants.
source: Of 35 participants, data from six participants had to be excluded from the final EEG data analysis due to technical issues during the EEG recording (i.e. the data of the excluded participants were contaminated with excessive muscle and/or technical artifacts) leaving a final sample of 29 participants.
evidence: Description of data exclusion and final sample size

claim: Thermal stimulation was performed using a 30 × 30 mm2 Peltier thermode at three different intensities: low heat (42°C), medium heat (46°C), and high heat (48°C).
source: Thermal stimulation was performed using a 30 × 30 mm2 Peltier thermode (CHEPS Pathway, Medoc) at three different intensities: low heat (42°C), medium heat (46°C), and high heat (48°C) at the left radial forearm.
evidence: Description of thermal stimulation parameters

claim: The three temperatures cover a large range of temperatures associated with nociception.
source: These three temperatures cover a large range of temperatures associated with nociception.
evidence: Justification for temperature selection

claim: The lowest temperature was set at 42°C to ensure a temperature above the median threshold of heat-sensitive C-fiber nociceptors which have a median heat threshold of 41°C.
source: The lowest temperature was set at 42°C to ensure a temperature above the median threshold of heat-sensitive C-fiber nociceptors which have a median heat threshold of 41°C (Treede et al., 1998).
evidence: Justification for lowest temperature based on nociceptor threshold from citation

claim: Aversive pictures were chosen from the International Affective Picture System (IAPS) database at three different levels of aversiveness.
source: Aversive pictures were chosen from the International Affective Picture System (IAPS) (Lang et al., 2008) database at three different levels of aversiveness.
evidence: Description of visual stimulus selection

claim: The color of the cue indicated the modality of the stimulus (orange for picture and blue for heat).
source: The color of the cue (triangle) indicated (probabilistically) the modality of the stimulus (orange for picture and blue for heat).
evidence: Description of cue design

claim: A white digit written inside of each triangle indicated the intensity of the subsequent stimulus (1, 2, and 3 for low, medium, and high intensity, respectively).
source: A white digit written inside of each triangle indicated (probabilistically) the intensity of the subsequent stimulus (1, 2, and 3 for low, medium, and high intensity, respectively).
evidence: Description of cue design

claim: EEG data were acquired using a 64-channel Ag/AgCl active electrode system placed according to the extended 10–20 system.
source: EEG data were acquired using a 64-channel Ag/AgCl active electrode system (ActiCap64; BrainProducts) placed according to the extended 10–20 system (Klem et al., 1999).
evidence: Description of EEG recording setup

claim: The EEG was sampled at 500 Hz, referenced at FCz, and grounded at Iz.
source: The EEG was sampled at 500 Hz, referenced at FCz, and grounded at Iz.
evidence: Description of EEG recording parameters

claim: Trials contaminated by eye-blinks and movements were corrected using an independent component analysis (ICA) algorithm.
source: Subsequently, trials contaminated by eye-blinks and movements were corrected using an independent component analysis (ICA) algorithm (Makeig et al., 1996; Jung et al., 2000).
evidence: Description of artifact correction method with citations

claim: Participants experienced a clear rating difference between the three levels of heat.
source: Our data show a clear rating difference between the three levels of heat.
evidence: Behavioral result from aversiveness ratings

claim: The main effect of stimulus intensity on aversiveness ratings was significant (F[1,28] = 743.97, p<0.001).
source: To evaluate the main effects of stimulus intensity, expectation, and absolute prediction errors, we employed a repeated-measures ANOVA of the behavioral data, which revealed significant effects for the main effect of stimulus intensity, that is, the three levels of heat (F[1,28] = 743.97, p<0.001).
evidence: Statistical result from repeated-measures ANOVA

claim: The main effect for expectation on aversiveness ratings was significant (F[1,28] = 38.53, p<0.001).
source: Also, the main effect for expectation on aversiveness ratings was significant (F[1,28] = 38.53, p<0.001) (Table 1), indicating an influence of the cued intensity on behavioral aversiveness ratings (Figure 4).
evidence: Statistical result from repeated-measures ANOVA

claim: The absolute prediction error showed only a trend effect on aversiveness ratings (F[1,28] = 2.87, p=0.10).
source: The absolute difference between the cued intensity and the actual stimulus intensity (i.e. absolute prediction error) only showed a trend effect on aversiveness ratings (F[1,28] = 2.87, p=0.10).
evidence: Statistical result from repeated-measures ANOVA

claim: A negative cluster in the low frequency range (1–30 Hz) was significantly associated with stimulus intensity, including samples from 250 to 1600 ms after stimulus onset (p=0.002).
source: Specifically, the negative cluster included samples in a time range from 250 to 1600 ms after stimulus onset in a frequency range from 1 to 30 Hz, predominately at contralateral central electrode sites (p=0.002).
evidence: EEG cluster analysis result

claim: A positive cluster in the low frequency range (1–30 Hz) was significantly associated with stimulus intensity, including samples from 150 to 1050 ms after stimulus onset in the theta frequency range (p=0.048).
source: Also in the low frequency range (1–30 Hz), a positive significant cluster included samples in a time range from 150 to 1050 ms after stimulus onset in the theta frequency range from 1 to 7 Hz predominately at midline electrode sites (p=0.048).
evidence: EEG cluster analysis result

claim: A positive cluster in the high frequency range (31–100 Hz) was significantly associated with stimulus intensity, including samples from 550 to 1600 ms after stimulus onset (p<0.001).
source: In the high frequency range (31–100 Hz) representing gamma activity, one positive cluster was significant (p<0.001). This cluster included samples in a time range from 550 to 1600 ms after stimulus onset and frequencies from 46 to 100 Hz, predominately at contralateral centroparietal electrode sites (Figure 5).
evidence: EEG cluster analysis result

claim: Higher intensity of thermal input is associated with increased theta and gamma band power.
source: In conclusion, these results indicate that a higher intensity of the thermal input is associated with increased theta and gamma band power and a negative relationship of alpha-to-beta band power and the intensity of the thermal input (see Figure 5 for a summary of the results of the main effect of stimulus intensity; see Figure 5—figure supplement 1 for single-subject differences in the gamma band between low stimulus intensity and high stimulus intensity trials).
evidence: Summary of EEG findings for stimulus intensity

claim: Higher intensity of thermal input is associated with a negative relationship of alpha-to-beta band power.
source: In conclusion, these results indicate that a higher intensity of the thermal input is associated with increased theta and gamma band power and a negative relationship of alpha-to-beta band power and the intensity of the thermal input (see Figure 5 for a summary of the results of the main effect of stimulus intensity; see Figure 5—figure supplement 1 for single-subject differences in the gamma band between low stimulus intensity and high stimulus intensity trials).
evidence: Summary of EEG findings for stimulus intensity

claim: One significant positive cluster in the low frequency range (1–30 Hz) was associated with cue intensity (expectation) (p=0.022).
source: This analysis revealed one significant positive cluster in the low frequency range (1–30 Hz), indicating a linear association of cue intensity (EXP) and power in this frequency range (p<0.05). The expectation cluster (p=0.022) included samples from time points ranging from 100 to 2000 ms after cue onset and included frequencies from 1 to 20 Hz.
evidence: EEG cluster analysis result for expectation

claim: An increase in alpha-to-beta band power is associated with experimental manipulation of expectations regarding the intensity of thermal input.
source: In summary, these results suggest an increase in alpha-to-beta band power to be associated with our experimental manipulation of expectations regarding the intensity of the thermal input.
evidence: Summary of EEG findings for expectation

claim: A significant negative cluster in the high frequency range (31–100 Hz) was associated with absolute prediction errors (p=0.002).
source: This analysis revealed a significant negative cluster in the high frequency range (31–100 Hz), indicating a (negative) linear association of absolute prediction errors and power in this frequency range (p=0.002). This (negative) absolute prediction error cluster included samples from frequencies ranging from 51 to 100 Hz and time points ranging from 50 to 1600 ms after stimulus onset.
evidence: EEG cluster analysis result for prediction errors

claim: A decrease in gamma band power is associated with experimental manipulation of expectation violations.
source: In summary, these results suggest a decrease in gamma band power to be associated with our experimental manipulation of expectation violations, resulting from a mismatch of the cued intensity and the actual heat input.
evidence: Summary of EEG findings for prediction errors

claim: A cluster analysis of the signed prediction error did not reveal any significant cluster of activity (all p>0.05).
source: A cluster analysis of the signed prediction error, stimulus-locked after stimulus onset (from 1 to 30 Hz for low frequencies and 31–100 Hz for gamma frequencies; from 0 to 1600 ms, stimulus-locked), did not reveal any significant cluster of activity associated with a linear increase or decrease of EXP (all p>0.05).
evidence: Negative result from cluster analysis

claim: A cluster analysis of the one-sided prediction error did not reveal any significant cluster of activity (all p>0.05).
source: Ignoring all stimulus–cue combinations of the PE where the stimulus intensity was less intense than expected leads to a one-sided PE. A cluster analysis of this effect did not reveal any significant cluster of activity (all p>0.05).
evidence: Negative result from cluster analysis

claim: In the reduced pain model, the main effect of stimulus intensity on pain ratings was significant (F[1,28] = 1109.9, p<0.001).
source: To evaluate the main effects of stimulus intensity, expectation, and absolute prediction errors in the behavioral data, we employed again a repeated-measures ANOVA which revealed significant effects for the main effect of stimulus intensity, that is, the two remaining levels of pain (F[1,28] = 1109.9, p<0.001).
evidence: Statistical result from reduced pain model analysis

claim: In the reduced pain model, the main effect for expectation on pain ratings was significant (F[1,28] = 17.07, p<0.001).
source: Also, the main effect for expectation on pain ratings was significant (F[1,28] = 17.07, p<0.001), indicating again an influence of the cued intensity on behavioral pain ratings.
evidence: Statistical result from reduced pain model analysis

claim: In the reduced pain model, the absolute prediction error revealed a positive significant effect on pain ratings (F[1,28] = 80.75, p<0.001).
source: The absolute difference between the cued intensity and the actual stimulus intensity (i.e. absolute prediction error) when only painful stimuli were included revealed a positive significant effect on pain ratings (F[1,28] = 80.75, p<0.001).
evidence: Statistical result from reduced pain model analysis

claim: The observed increase in theta power agrees with previous studies and most likely corresponds to pain-related evoked potentials.
source: Therefore, our observed increase in theta power agrees with previous studies (Ploner et al., 2017) and most likely correspond to pain-related evoked potentials (Lorenz and Garcia-Larrea, 2003; Tiemann et al., 2015), such as the P2 with a similar topography.
evidence: Interpretation of findings in context of previous literature

claim: The observed suppression of alpha-to-beta activity is in line with reported beta suppression in previous EEG studies on pain.
source: In addition, we observed a significant suppression of alpha-to-beta activity which, given the abovementioned delays of our painful stimuli, is in line with the reported beta suppression in previous EEG studies on pain (Mouraux et al., 2003; Ploner et al., 2006; May et al., 2012; Hu et al., 2013).
evidence: Interpretation of findings in context of previous literature

claim: Power in the gamma band was correlated with heat intensity, which is in line with previous studies.
source: Finally, power in the gamma band was also correlated with heat intensity, which is in line with previous studies (Gross et al., 2007; Hauck et al., 2007; Zhang et al., 2012; Rossiter et al., 2013; Tiemann et al., 2015).
evidence: Interpretation of findings in context of previous literature

claim: Only the alpha-to-beta band desynchronization differentiated between medium and high pain conditions.
source: Interestingly, only the alpha-to-beta band desynchronization differentiated between medium and high pain conditions, whereas differences in the theta and gamma band activity were only evident when the lowest stimulus intensity was included which was perceived as neutral.
evidence: Observation from data analysis comparing different frequency bands

claim: The effect of prediction errors on perception increased when the analysis was constrained to clearly painful stimuli.
source: Interestingly, the effect of prediction errors on perception increased, and became significant, when we constrained our analysis to the clearly painful stimuli (reduced pain model).
evidence: Comparison between full model and reduced pain model results

claim: A prediction error seems to more strongly affect pain perception than thermoception.
source: This suggests that a prediction error seems to more strongly affect pain perception, whereas the effect is weaker in the context of thermoception.
evidence: Interpretation of differences between full and reduced models

claim: Feedforward connections are predominately originating from superficial layers and feedback connections from deep layers in cortical microcircuits.
source: Theoretical accounts (Arnal and Giraud, 2012; Bastos et al., 2012) have suggested that predictive coding mechanisms could be related to the functional architecture of neuronal microcircuits. As feedforward connections are predominately originating from superficial layers and feedback connections from deep layers, it has been suggested that prediction errors should be expressed by higher frequencies than the predictions that accumulate them.
evidence: Theoretical framework from cited literature

claim: In the auditory modality, prediction errors in the context of repetition suppression were associated with higher gamma band activity.
source: In the auditory modality, these ideas are supported by empirical data (Todorovic et al., 2011) showing that prediction errors in the context of repetition suppression were associated with higher gamma band activity.
evidence: Empirical finding from cited auditory study

claim: In the visual domain, temporo-parietal beta power was correlated with the predictability of an action kinematics–outcome sequence, while gamma power was correlated with the prediction error.
source: Likewise, in the visual domain, an MEG study has shown that temporo-parietal beta power was correlated with the predictability of an action kinematics–outcome sequence, while gamma power was correlated with the prediction error (van Pelt et al., 2016).
evidence: Empirical finding from cited visual MEG study

claim: In rodents, an information flow between S1 gamma and ACC beta activity has been suggested during spontaneous pain.
source: A recent study in rodents has suggested an information flow between S1 gamma and ACC (Anterior Cingulate Cortex) beta activity during spontaneous pain (Xiao et al., 2019).
evidence: Finding from cited rodent study

claim: In humans, the sensorimotor cortex is more strongly connected to the medial prefrontal cortex at alpha frequencies during tonic pain.
source: Finally, in humans, a recent EEG study showed that the sensorimotor cortex is more strongly connected to the medial prefrontal cortex at alpha frequencies during tonic pain, suggesting alpha band activity in tonic pain to be associated with bottom-up instead of top-down signaling (Nickel et al., 2020).
evidence: Finding from cited human EEG study

claim: Alpha suppression in the anterior insula is related mainly to pain expectation.
source: In particular, a previous MEG study reported that alpha suppression in the anterior insula is related mainly to pain expectation in a paradigm in which painful stimuli were interleaved with non-painful stimuli (Franciotti et al., 2009).
evidence: Finding from cited MEG study

claim: Alpha desynchronization in the context of predictable painful stimuli has been discussed as a possible neural correlate of attentional preparatory processes.
source: In a related study, alpha desynchronization in the context of predictable painful stimuli has been discussed as a possible neural correlate of attentional preparatory processes (Babiloni et al., 2003).
evidence: Interpretation from cited study

claim: Resting-state alpha band activity was linked to the expectation of pain modulation (analgesia) in a placebo paradigm.
source: A previous study reported that resting-state alpha band activity was also linked to the expectation of pain modulation (analgesia) in a placebo paradigm (Huneke et al., 2013).
evidence: Finding from cited placebo study

claim: Pain modulation due to nocebo expectation is associated with enhanced alpha activity.
source: With respect to negative expectations, it has been shown that pain modulation due to nocebo expectation is associated with enhanced alpha activity (Albu and Meagher, 2016).
evidence: Finding from cited nocebo study

claim: The findings indicate an important role of low frequency activity in mediating expectation effects in a pain network underlying a generative model for pain perception.
source: Our findings are in line with these results indicating an important role of low frequency activity in mediating expectation effects in a pain network underlying a generative model for pain perception.
evidence: Interpretation of current findings in context of literature

claim: Increased gamma power has been associated with successful matching between external input and internal representation.
source: For instance, increased gamma power has been associated with successful matching (i.e. the absence of a prediction error) between external input and internal representation (Herrmann et al., 2004a; Osipova et al., 2006; Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: Finding from cited studies on gamma activity

claim: Gamma band responses have been explained in terms of the match between bottom-up and top-down information.
source: In particular, gamma band responses have been explained in terms of the match between bottom-up and top-down information (Herrmann et al., 2004b).
evidence: Theoretical interpretation from cited study

claim: A critical word that is semantically predictable by the preceding sentence induces a larger gamma response than words which are semantically incongruent.
source: It has been shown that a critical word that is semantically predictable by the preceding sentence (so-called high cloze probability) induces a larger gamma response than words which are semantically incongruent (i.e. unpredicted; low cloze probability) (Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: Finding from cited language comprehension study

claim: The lowest stimulus intensity was often not perceived as painful but as hot.
source: In the present study, the lowest stimulus intensity was often not perceived as painful but as hot.
evidence: Observation from behavioral data

claim: Even though the lowest stimulus intensity (42°C) was above the threshold of nociceptors, the subjective experience was often rated as neutral.
source: Therefore, we performed an additional analysis (reduced pain model) only comprising clearly painful stimuli (46°C and 48°C) to more specifically address expectations and predictions errors in pain. The analyses of the behavioral data revealed similar results. Both models showed a highly significant effect of stimulus intensity and expectation on perceived stimulus intensity. In addition, the reduced pain model showed a significant prediction error effect, which was formally not observed in the full model. However, it is important to note that this difference should not be overinterpreted, as the p-value for the prediction error effect of the full model was at a trend level (p=0.1). Importantly, the negative representation of prediction errors in the gamma band was evident in both, the reduced and the full model.
evidence: Observation from behavioral data and justification for reduced model

claim: The study was restricted to male participants, which means the results cannot be generalized to the population.
source: We therefore decided to also keep the sample characteristics similar and restricted the sample to male participants, which means that we cannot generalize our results to the population.
evidence: Acknowledgment of study limitation

claim: The study used a four-button device to assess stimulus intensity, being limited to a coarse rating scale of four levels.
source: To minimize motor responses and speed up the rating procedure, we used a four-button device to directly assess stimulus intensity (in contrast to using two buttons to move a slider on a VAS), thus being limited to a coarse rating scale of four levels, where one was labeled as 'neutral' and four was labeled as 'very strong'.
evidence: Description of methodological choice and limitation

claim: Key variables required for pain perception and thermoception in the context of a generative model are correlated with distinct oscillatory profiles in the brain.
source: Our data show that key variables required for pain perception and thermoception in the context of a generative model are correlated with distinct oscillatory profiles in the brain.
evidence: Summary conclusion from the study

claim: Each oscillatory frequency band was correlated with a distinct variable such as expectation and prediction errors.
source: Furthermore, each oscillatory frequency band was correlated with a distinct variable such as expectation and prediction errors.
evidence: Summary conclusion from the study
